for-loops-over-text.label: For Loops Over Text
for-loops-over-text.summary: Use a `for` loop to visit a string one character at a time, work with the current loop variable, and select or transform characters directly.

sc-1.title: What does the loop visit?
sc-1.prompt: In Python, what does `for ch in "dog":` loop over?
sc-1.hint: A string supplies one character to the loop variable at a time.

help.concept: Iterating directly over a string visits its characters from left to right.
help.hint_1: For `"dog"`, the values are `"d"`, then `"o"`, then `"g"`.
help.hint_2: The loop variable does not hold the entire string at once.

sc-2.title: What prints?
sc-2.prompt:
What is printed by this code?

```python
for ch in "hi":
    print(ch)
```
sc-2.hint: The loop runs once for `h` and once for `i`.

help.concept: `print(ch)` prints the current character during each repetition.
help.hint_1: Each `print` call ends its own output line.
help.hint_2: The characters keep their original order.

options.c: h on one line, then i on the next line

sketch-1.title: Visit each character from left to right
sketch-1.bodyMarkdown:
A string is a sequence of characters, so a `for` loop can visit those characters directly.

```python
word = "cat"

for ch in word:
    print(ch)
```

The output is:

```text
c
a
t
```

Python does not need an index or `range()` here. The string itself supplies the loop values.

The loop runs once for each character, in order from left to right.

sketch-2.title: Use the current character inside the loop
sketch-2.bodyMarkdown:
The loop variable holds one character at a time.

```python
text = "go"

for ch in text:
    print(ch.upper())
```

The first repetition uses `"g"`, then the second uses `"o"`.

Output:

```text
G
O
```

The loop variable can be named `ch`, `letter`, `char`, or another valid variable name. What matters is that it represents the **current character** during that repetition.

You can use normal string operations on that character before printing it.

sketch-3.title: Select characters with a condition
sketch-3.bodyMarkdown:
You can combine a text loop with an `if` statement when only some characters should produce output.

```python
text = "banana"

for ch in text:
    if ch in "aeiou":
        print(ch)
```

The output is:

```text
a
a
a
```

The loop still visits every character. The condition decides whether the current character should be printed.

This is **selection**, not accumulation: the program handles each character directly instead of building a running count or result.

Counting matches and building running results belong in the next lesson on accumulators and counters.
